That's all I'm saying. Now, I don't think that's true about Christianity. There are some things that, I don't know if you'd call them anomalies, I don't know if I'd call them anomalies. Maybe I did back then, Scott. I wouldn't call them anomalies now. I would call them probably mysteries, but I don't think you can just take an apparent contradiction and just dismiss it. No, let me back up. You can't take a contradiction and dismiss it by calling it a mystery. So when an atheist says there's evil in the world, that's a contradiction. And it's not enough for him to say, well, that's just a mystery. It's not a mystery. We can understand why there's evil in the world. It's because there's a standard of good, and we can understand where the standard of good comes from, because there is a God whose moral nature is the standard for moral perfection. And that's the standard by which we measure good and evil. Makes perfect sense. It's not an anomaly, and it's not contradictory. The atheist wants to go that direction, he's going to live with a contradiction. And you can't just call it a mystery. Now, I do think there are mysteries. That is, and we do talk about this on occasion. I think Amy and I did a show this morning where we talked about this. How does God's perfect control over all that happens over all time, over everything, how does that work with freedom of the will? Now, I think that's an anomaly, an anomaly. And there are people who've kind of worked with it more than I have to kind of show how this all works together. It's not strict determinism, and it's not God completely out of control. There's some middle ground. Where is that middle ground? I don't know. And there is speculation on how that might work, but it's mysterious. It is anomalous. It's unusual, but it's not contradictory. Because I think there is certainly a way human beings can be free and God can be in control. I just don't know how that works. Now, maybe people are thinking, you're just playing games with words. You know, that's just as much a contradiction as anything else. Well, what are the alternatives? If there is no God, if there is a God, he's going to have to be sovereign, because that's one of the characteristics of God. He's like the one. He's not limited. He's not finite. It's not adequate to the task. But if there is no God, then you've got just molecules in motion governed by natural law, so you have no freedom there either. Everything is determined by the necessary and sufficient prior conditions that determines them. So what's the option? What are the alternatives? That's the question I'm asking here. Yes, there are some things that seem anomalous, very few, now when I get down to it, but in Christian theology. But there's always going to be mystery in the world. What I can't live with is a direct contradiction, and I think that's what atheists run into in a number of circumstances. There is no explanation for how this took place given atheism or how this could be the case given atheism. Alright? So I hope that's helpful. Scott, we've got another question from Laurie here. This is interesting. I've never had this question before. You got Laurie? Yeah. Go ahead, Laurie. Hi, Greg. This is Laurie. I've called in before. I have a question about church. I do not like going to church. I love the sermons, but I do not like the service. I'm a musician, and most of the music they play there is extremely repetitive, and I don't like it. And a lot of sort of perfunctory, repetitive, apostle's creed statements, and on and on and on and on. And then I think the last straw for me, which made me stop going and just listening to the sermons on YouTube, is when they're trying to raise $11 million for a new building, and they've already got a ton of buildings, which I felt like could have been raised to help the community, but whatever. Anyway, in the sermon they were talking about the story and acts of Ananias and how the people lied about their donation to the apostles. And I always thought that story was about lying and deception. And he just kind of joked about our donations to this building project. And it's just, the whole thing just turned me off. And I'm just, I don't like going to church. I'm sorry. Like I said, I love the sermons. I watch tons of sermons all the time, but the service is just terrible. So I just wondered if you had any advice for me. Thank you so much. Bye. Well, Laurie, thanks for your candidness about this. It sounds to me that the problem isn't that you don't like going to church. It sounds to me like the church that you're going to, you don't like. And from what you described, I wouldn't like them either. Now, you mentioned the sermons are great. Maybe you meant when I have the freedom to go online and listen to any teacher I want to listen to, then the sermons are great, but I would be surprised if the sermons were great from the pastor who is leading the church you just described. I am sympathetic to some degree, some modest degree, to the opening concerns that you raised, like the worship was not satisfying. I have been to churches where the worship was fabulous and the preaching was poor, and other churches where the preaching was fabulous and the worship was poor, partly for the reasons that you mentioned. Some of the songs just seemed to be, what is the word, dreary. That's it. Dreary. Like they were funeral dirges or something, you know. Or all the repetition. Some people have called those 7-Eleven songs. Seven words repeated eleven times. You know. Now, I was at a church last week, though, and they had a repetition of a certain phrase or a refrain, and I thought it was very effective, frankly. This was the church that has particularly good worship. It's a larger church with a worship team. They do a great job. So I get uplifted by that kind of thing. Sometimes when you have a smaller worship team because you have a smaller church, you just have a smaller group to draw talent from, and they just aren't that talented. And I think the times when I've thought of the worship being less than ideal, it's when they've been smaller churches, and you kind of go with what you got. People are willing to volunteer to lead the worship. Now, I have been in those circumstances quite often and have been less than inspired by the worship, but I have to put it up to the Lord and say, hey, you know, maybe they're doing the best they can.

There are certain styles of worship that I don't care for, and that's when you lose the harmony and you lose the beauty from a song that otherwise would be beautiful and harmonious and attractive and sweet and lovely and worshipful. And then all of that goodness gets strained out of it by a style of the worship leader. We can do without that. But nevertheless, you're probably always going to have a mixed bag with whatever church you go to. Laurie, I don't think it's a good idea that you just get your sermons online because that's not church. That's sermons. That's teaching. It's great, but it's not church. Church comes from the Greek word ekklesia, and that literally means the called-out ones. And there's probably a double meaning there. These are the ones called out of the world in a certain sense to be together, called out to be together. And the second sense is, and I'm not sure if this was intended, but it certainly fits, we come out from the world on a given day to be together. But the key is that we are together. We are not on our own. And we are gathered together with, you know, the good, the bad, and the ugly, so to speak. And we carry on with each other, even though there are things that we don't like about it. I think from what you described in that church, Laurie, you had a bad actor church. This was not a good thing. Now, all churches are going to expect that the people who benefit from what they do, presuming there's a benefit, should share financially with them. You pay your dues. That's standard. We have the same general attitude here at Stand to Reason. If you benefit from us, we'll offer it freely without charge. But if you benefit, it makes sense for you then to give back, and that's what strategic partners often will say. We love giving to you because it's a give-take relationship. It's a quid pro quo, this for that. And the worker is worthy of his wages. So I'm not troubled that a church would campaign for funds for their needs. Now, whether those funds are being well spent, that's another question. And I don't know, in this particular case, you've got a big church and you want $11 million, that'll buy a lot of buildings. But I can't assess because I don't know the circumstances there. Obviously, you were troubled by that. And if you think this is not a good use of funds by the leaders and there was manipulation, find another church. But if you find another church, they're still going to want you to participate financially, and they should. There's nothing wrong with that, as long as it's not illicit and out of hand, and the money is used well to feed the flock, the called-out ones. Now, as far as the worship and the preaching is concerned, it makes little sense to go to a church where the preaching is not feeding you well. It might be that the worship doesn't help you, and you can get worship other places. And I would have to, in the circumstances I described, I just have to sit through the worship that I didn't care for and try to enter in the songs that I could robustly enter into, and the other ones I would just be silent and pray about stuff, sometimes for the worship team, sometimes for myself and my attitude, that I, oh Lord, I'm just being judgmental again, critical again. Oh, I'm sorry, but the music is so bad, Lord. So anyway, that's the way I deal with it. Somebody put it this way. They said, don't look for a perfect church. If you found it, they wouldn't let you join anyway. You'd mess it up. Who was it? Groucho Marx said that I never belonged to an organization that would have me as a member. Or maybe there was a variation. I really liked this girl until I asked her out, and she agreed, then I lost respect for her. I mean, it's the kind of corny ways of saying the same thing. Every individual is going to mess up a church to some degree because none of us are perfect, and certainly the churches that we go to aren't going to be perfect. But you should find a church that you are willing to go to and be part of because it gives you enough for you to be satisfied to be part of that community. And that's the important part here, Laurie, the community. I have had, in the past, really mixed feelings about going to church on Sundays, and sometimes with traveling and everything, and then finally I get a Sunday where I can be with my family at church, you know, it's like, oh, I want to sleep in. That's what I want to do. Part of me does. But you know, when I decide to, you know, break the spell, get out of bed, get cleaned up, go to church, I'm always glad I did, even if the worship isn't up to snuff by my standards. I'm always glad I did. Being a member of the ekklesia, the called-out ones, I am not only receiving by being there in some measure, but I'm also there to give, to be a member of that community that encourages others as I have opportunity. So there's a two-way element there with church attendance. Now, there may be other things you don't like. You might be at a liturgical church and they're kind of droning on about the Apostles' Creed. Okay, I think it's really sad when really important things like creeds are used in church and it's droned on, because those things are rich. They're theologically rich, and they can be really helpful for people. But if it becomes rote, it loses its power. And this is going to require vigilance on all of our part who are involved in that local congregation to try to keep it alive, but don't just make your church, so to speak, through the video. That's not church because it's not community. It may be a sermon, it may be worship, and you're doing it all by yourself. Some people have no other choice. They're bedridden, or they're in locations totally away from something where this is the way they can get fed, but they're not in community, so it's not ideal. It is better for you to be in community that's harder for you. That might be good for your character to put up with other people in the community that aren't just so. I mean, that's part of the way God used it in my own life. So anyway, Laurie, I hope that helps. Please go back to church or find a church that you're willing to go back to and be part of that community. All right, friends, thank you for being with me today. I'm Greg Koukl for Stand to Reason. Give them heaven, friends. Bye-bye now.
